guide.title: Game guide
guide.intro: Everything you need for your road to legend. No help is ever announced: your decisions really count.
guide.b.career: Choose player or coach, your path (European academy, draft or undrafted) and your first club. Each week you play a round; the season ends with playoffs and awards. You can cross between Europe and the NBA.
guide.b.week: On HOME you set the plan: extra training improves attributes but loads your body; resting recovers. The form, morale, fitness, coach and fans bars sum up your moment.
guide.b.live: Play live and the game stops at key moments: opposing runs, foul trouble, final minutes, last possession or tactical fouls. If you take the last shot yourself, you decide it with the buzzer-beater minigame.
guide.b.decisions: Agent, sponsorship, press, locker room, contracts… Some options are sure things and others show a percentage. Several decisions come back weeks later.
guide.b.minigames: In ME: free throws, three-point contest, buzzer beater, dunks, defence and 1-on-1. Release when the cursor is in the green zone. Automatic mode gives a solid standard result.
guide.b.pet: Three care actions per week, cuddles and basketball tricks. A happy pet lifts your morale; a neglected one drags it down. Every four weeks you can enter a contest.
guide.b.playoffs: NBA: play-in and best-of-7 series. Liga Endesa: top 8. Primera FEB: 1st goes up directly, the rest play the promotion playoff. At the end come MVP, best defender, rookie, sixth man, most improved and the all-league team.
guide.b.coach: In ME you pick the starting five and tactics (pace, offense and defense). On HOME you set the week's load and read the scouting report.
guide.b.saves: The game saves automatically on every action. In MORE › Saves you have 10 slots and exportable backups. Works offline.
guide.b.a11y: In Settings: large text, high contrast, colour-blind mode, reduced motion and optional sound. Every minigame has an automatic mode.

inbox.eraRule.quarters: New rule: games are now played in quarters.
era.d.1920sDesc: Small wooden courts, a laced leather ball and two-handed set shots. No shot clock, no three-point line: scores rarely top 40.
era.d.1930sDesc: FIBA is founded (1932) and basketball enters the 1936 Olympics, with an outdoor final. The one-handed shot starts to appear.
era.d.1940sDesc: Modern professional leagues are born. The jump shot spreads and tall centres rule the paint. Still no shot clock.
era.d.1950sDesc: The North American league adopts 24 seconds (1954) and FIBA 30 seconds (1956). No more freezing the ball; games speed up.
era.d.1960sDesc: Fast breaks, jump shots and television entering the arenas. Two 20-minute halves in FIBA basketball.
era.d.1970sDesc: Afros, dunks and tube socks. Women's basketball debuts at the 1976 Olympics and in 1979 the North American league introduces the three.
era.d.1980sDesc: FIBA approves the three at 6.25 m (1984). Shooters become weapons and rivalries fill the arenas.
era.d.1990sDesc: Professionals reach the Olympics (1992) and basketball goes worldwide. The three becomes routine.
era.d.2000sDesc: FIBA moves to four 10-minute quarters and a 24-second clock (2000). More possessions, more athleticism.
era.d.2010sDesc: The FIBA line moves back to 6.75 m (2010). Data rules: threes, layups and free throws.
era.d.2020sDesc: Today's rules: the game you already know, with every record still to break.
